And it is ten gold coins. The Gemara in Chullin concludes that the ten gold coins compensate for the blessing over covering the blood. For Grace after Meals the amount is forty gold coins for four blessings. The Ran holds that compensation also applies for loss of the commandment itself. This is not contradicted by the fact that only ten coins are paid for covering the blood, because where the blessing cannot exist apart from the commandment the two are not assessed separately. Tosafot asks why Grace after Meals is not worth fifty coins, including the blessing over wine, and answers that the view in question does not require a new blessing over the cup. I suggest instead that only Torah-level blessings generate this fixed liability. The fourth blessing of Grace after Meals was instituted at Yavneh and is rabbinic, so together with the blessing over wine the count remains four. This also reconciles Rif and Rosh, who require a blessing over the cup yet record only forty coins. Rabbeinu Yerucham cites Rav Tzemach similarly, though elsewhere he explains that the wine blessing is omitted because it is a blessing over enjoyment, in which case the fourth blessing is included. Either explanation may accord with Rif and Rosh.
If he had a son to circumcise, etc. He is exempt. The Sema distinguishes between the father and another mohel regarding answering Amen, but this distinction is not persuasive. Rabbeinu Yerucham states that where the displaced person could answer Amen, the one who performed the circumcision is exempt even when the father himself was obligated. If the father assigned another mohel and a third person performed the circumcision first, the designated mohel acquired no proprietary right in the commandment; even a formal act of acquisition would be merely an acquisition of words. This is explicit in the Rosh and is the basis of the ruling in Yoreh Deah. The father himself, however, should circumcise his son when capable, just as the one who slaughtered should cover the blood. The Gemara and Rambam place the obligation first upon the father, and those who routinely honor another while able to perform it themselves forgo a great positive commandment. Maharashal argues that even if the father answered Amen, the interloper remains liable because the commandment itself was taken, but Tosafot, Rosh, Mordechai, Ran, and the other authorities correctly hold that answering Amen gives equivalent reward and removes the loss. Rabban Gamliel's case must therefore involve circumstances in which the displaced person could not answer Amen, such as a blessing recited quietly. The same analysis applies to Grace after Meals and Torah blessings. The common saying that honoring another with Grace after Meals gives him forty gold coins is imprecise where the one honoring can answer Amen; at most it gives precedence in reward. If one actually prevented him from hearing or answering and thereby took the public blessing, the fixed payment may apply. Regarding purchased synagogue honors, Maharashal suggests that one who preempts the purchaser may owe ten gold coins if the purchaser seized them, but this is not conclusive. See Maharashal for additional distinctions.
“And it is ten gold coins.” In the Gemara, chapter Kisui HaDam, folio 87a, the conclusion is that this amount is compensation for the blessing over covering the blood. With Grace After Meals one must pay forty gold coins for the four blessings. Lechem Chamudot, chapter Kisui HaDam, beginning of folio 192, cites the Ran that compensation is also paid for deprivation of the mitzvah itself, and asks: if covering the blood has both the mitzvah and the blessing, why does he pay only ten gold coins rather than compensation for both? He leaves the matter requiring study. There is no difficulty. The Ran’s position is proved by the Gemara at the end of HaChovel, Tosafot there, and many other authorities, all of whom explicitly write that deprivation of a mitzvah itself requires ten gold coins. Yet with covering the blood the total remains only ten. Necessarily, the reason is that the blessing cannot be separated from the mitzvah. Since the blessing exists only together with the act of covering, the two are valued as one loss for purposes of the ten gold coins.
Tosafot in the chapter Kisui HaDam write: “One might ask that the amount should have been fifty gold coins, since there is also the blessing over the wine. One can answer that Rabbi follows the opinion that one need not recite a new blessing over the cup of Grace After Meals, but relies on the blessing over the first cup.” Thus far Tosafot. This is difficult to me. The Gemara says there that Rabbi asked him, “Will you drink the cup of blessing, or will you take forty gold coins?” This plainly implies that there was indeed a blessing over the cup, since it calls it a “cup of blessing.” It is strained to say that it is called that only because Grace After Meals is recited over it. There is a further difficulty. In Arvei Pesachim, Pesachim 103, the Amoraim themselves disagree whether a new blessing is required over that cup. Rabbi’s incident would then contradict the Amora who requires the blessing. It is strained to answer that the dispute there involves students of Rav whereas Rabbi was a Tanna who could disagree. In my humble opinion, the answer is instead that the obligation of ten gold coins applies only to a Torah-level mitzvah or blessing, not a rabbinic one. Maharshal writes in the chapter HaChovel, siman 60, that deprivation of a rabbinic mitzvah does not generate this payment. The blessing HaTov VeHaMetiv was instituted at Yavneh and is only rabbinic. Thus, together with the blessing over wine, there are still only four blessings that count for compensation. This explanation is also necessary according to Rif and the Rosh. In Arvei Pesachim they rule that one must recite a blessing over the cup of Grace After Meals. Yet at the end of Kisui HaDam they cite the incident where Rabban Gamliel required payment of ten gold coins for a blessing, and the incident where Rabbi said, “Will you drink the cup of blessing or take forty gold coins?” The implication is that the total is only forty. Accordingly, Tosafot’s answer cannot explain their position. Rather, the explanation must be as I have written: the fourth blessing of Grace After Meals, HaTov VeHaMetiv, is rabbinic and does not count, while the blessing over the wine does. Thus the total remains four compensable blessings. This appears correct.
I subsequently found that Rabbeinu Yerucham, Sefer Adam, Netiv 15, part 4, writes exactly as I did, and I was pleased. He cites Rav Tzemach: “It is difficult to me that they say the value is forty gold coins corresponding to four blessings. There are really five: the four blessings of Grace After Meals and one over the wine. I answer that they counted only the three blessings of Grace After Meals that are of Torah origin and did not count the fourth because it is rabbinic.” Thus far his words. However, in Sefer Meisharim, in the laws of damages, Netiv 31, end of part 4, Rabbeinu Yerucham writes: “A cup of blessing is worth forty gold coins. The blessing over the fruit of the vine is not included in the count, because it is a blessing over enjoyment.” Thus far his words. According to this latter explanation, HaTov VeHaMetiv is included among the four. It is possible that Rif and the Rosh likewise understand the matter this way.
“If he had a son to circumcise, etc., he is exempt.” The Sema writes: “See Yoreh Deah, end of siman 28, where it states that even if the injured party seized payment, we remove it from him, because he answered Amen, and one who answers Amen is greater than the one who recites the blessing. If he heard and failed to answer, he caused his own loss. But with a father, answering Amen does not help.” He then criticizes Ir Shushan for giving different reasons why the person who preempted the circumcision is exempt and says that Ir Shushan failed to consider the ruling at the end of siman 28. The Sema’s words are not correct. There is no reason to distinguish regarding answering Amen between a father and anyone else. This is explicit in Rabbeinu Yerucham, the source of the present ruling. He writes that whenever the person could answer Amen, the preemptor is exempt even where the mitzvah rests personally upon the father. In Netiv 31, end of part 4, he writes: “If one told a mohel to circumcise and another person preempted him and circumcised, the latter is exempt. But if he took the mitzvah from the father himself, he is liable. Likewise, one who prevents an owner from performing a mitzvah and preempts him must pay ten gold coins; and if the injured party seized payment we do not remove it from him, except where he could answer Amen.” Thus far his words. Maharshal in the chapter HaChovel, siman 60, likewise explicitly makes no distinction between a father and another person. The same follows from Ma'adanei Yom Tov and from the Sema’s own Perishah, whom I cite below. They explain that in the incident involving Rabban Gamliel the other person must have recited the blessing quietly. Had he recited it aloud, the injured party could have answered Amen and the preemptor would have been exempt. Yet with covering the blood, the mitzvah rests personally upon the one who slaughtered just as circumcision rests upon the father, for Scripture says, “the one who spills the blood shall cover it.” This proves that there is no distinction. Accordingly, Ir Shushan’s explanation is correct, and the Sema’s criticism is unwarranted. Ir Shushan writes: “This applies specifically where the father himself wished to circumcise, since the Torah obligates him. But if the father gave the child to another person to circumcise and someone else preempted him, the preemptor is exempt toward the father because he did not deprive the father of the mitzvah, and exempt toward the appointed mohel because by what act did that mohel acquire the mitzvah? Even if the father made a formal kinyan with him, it is ineffective, because it is merely a kinyan concerning words.” Thus far Ir Shushan. This is precisely the Rosh’s position at the end of Kisui HaDam. The Rosh first cites Rabbeinu Tam, who exempted a mohel who preempted another person to whom a child had been entrusted, both because fines are not collected nowadays and because the injured party could have answered Amen. The Rosh then adds: “Even without Rabbeinu Tam’s reasons, it appears to me that the mohel is exempt. Although the father told another mohel to circumcise his son, that mohel acquired no legal right in the mitzvah that would obligate a third person who preempted him. This is unlike covering the blood, where Scripture says, ‘the one who slaughtered shall cover,’ so the one who slaughtered has the right to cover. Likewise, if a father, who is obligated to circumcise his son, wished to do so himself and another preempted him, the latter is liable. But if the father does not wish to circumcise personally, all Israel are obligated to circumcise the child, and the father’s mere words to one mohel do not vest that mohel with a compensable right against another who preempts him.” Thus far the Rosh. This is exactly Ir Shushan’s explanation. Rabbeinu Yerucham’s ruling above is clearly taken from this Rosh. The Rosh also writes in responsa, rule 12, siman 3, that even if the father makes a kinyan with the mohel concerning the circumcision, it is ineffective because it is a kinyan concerning mere words. The Rama records this at the beginning of Yoreh Deah siman 264. As for the Sema’s supposed proof from the end of Yoreh Deah siman 28—that exemption there is because the injured party could answer Amen, implying that otherwise the preemptor would be liable—it is no proof. The Beit Yosef and the Sema’s own Perishah already note there that this language is not from the Tur but was added by another hand. The Tur necessarily holds that the preemptor is exempt independently because the originally designated person acquired no right, in accordance with the Rosh. There is no doubt that the Rosh’s words escaped the Sema here. Had he seen them, he would not have written this criticism. Maharshal likewise rules in HaChovel, siman 60, in accordance with the Rosh, that the preemptor is exempt because the other mohel acquired no right in the mitzvah.
The Rama and Ir Shushan here therefore speak of a situation where the injured party could not answer Amen—for example, the preemptor pushed him away or recited the blessing quietly. The Rosh’s words that I cited also prove that a father who is himself a competent mohel should not give his son to another person to circumcise. The father is personally obligated, just as the person who slaughtered is personally obligated to cover the blood. Rambam likewise writes at the beginning of Hilkhot Milah that this positive commandment rests first upon the father. The plain Gemara in Kiddushin 29a says the same: “The father is obligated to circumcise his son. From where do we know this? Because it is written, ‘Avraham circumcised his son Yitzchak.’ If the father did not circumcise him, beit din is obligated to do so.” I write this because I have seen many people honor others with circumcising their sons even though they themselves know how to perform the circumcision. In my view, they thereby neglect a positive commandment and a very great mitzvah of circumcision, and beit din should abolish this practice.
Maharshal writes in the chapter HaChovel, siman 60: “According to Rabbeinu Tam’s reason for exempting the mohel, even if the injured party seized payment we remove it from him, because he answered Amen, and one who answers Amen is greater than the one who recites the blessing. If he failed to answer Amen, he caused his own loss. Necessarily, therefore, the incident of Rabban Gamliel, where another person covered the blood without the first person’s consent, must concern a case where the preemptor recited the blessing quietly so that the other could not hear, or pushed him away so that he could not hear. This does not appear correct to me. The Gemara states the rule without qualification, and ordinarily one recites a blessing in the usual manner. Certainly the case should not be understood as involving wicked people deliberately preventing another from answering Amen. Rather, even if the injured party answered Amen, the preemptor remains liable. The rule that one who answers Amen is greater than the person reciting the blessing applies where there is no separate mitzvah-act, such as the blessing over Torah reading or prayer, where the only deprivation is the blessing itself. Covering the blood and circumcision, however, are independent positive commandments and the blessing is not indispensable. The preemptor deprived the other person of the mitzvah itself. Although we do not assess the mitzvah and blessing separately as two sets of ten gold coins, the mitzvah alone is itself worth ten gold coins, just like the cases of the ox and the tree discussed above. Therefore, if he seized ten gold coins even nowadays, we do not remove them from him. Although a great tree has ruled otherwise and pillars of the world—Tosafot, the Rosh, Mordekhai, and the Ran—depend upon it, I fear lest my skull be crushed by disagreeing; nevertheless, it is Torah and I must study, and I have written what appears to me.” Thus far Maharshal. His words are not correct. The position of Tosafot, the Rosh, Mordekhai at the end of Kisui HaDam, the Tur in Yoreh Deah at the end of siman 28 in the name of Mahari Chizkiyah’s rulings, and their supporters is the word of the living God. The Gemara at the end of Kisui HaDam itself asks, regarding the incident of Rabban Gamliel, whether the ten gold coins are compensation for the mitzvah or for the blessing, and resolves that they are compensation for the blessing from the incident involving Grace After Meals in Rabbi’s house, where the amount was forty gold coins. Thus, even though covering the blood and circumcision involve both a mitzvah and a blessing, the principal compensable deprivation is the blessing. Moreover, regardless of the theoretical reason, since one who answers Amen is greater than the person reciting the blessing and thereby receives the reward represented by the ten gold coins, the preemptor has caused him no loss. Why should he be liable? Necessarily, the incident of Rabban Gamliel concerns a case where the other person could not answer Amen. This is not at all strained or dependent upon assuming wicked conduct. We need not say that the preemptor deliberately whispered the blessing so the other would not hear or physically pushed him away. The case can simply be that he naturally recited the blessing quietly. Ma'adanei Yom Tov at the end of Kisui HaDam likewise writes that Rabbeinu Tam exempted the competing mohel because circumcision blessings are generally said aloud, allowing the other to answer Amen, whereas the blessing over covering blood is commonly recited quietly. The Perishah at the end of Yoreh Deah siman 28 writes the same.
Ma'adanei Yom Tov, at the end of the chapter Kisui HaDam, asks about Rabbeinu Tam’s reason for exempting the preempting mohel because the other person could have answered Amen. At the end of the chapter Elu Devarim, and likewise at the end of Sotah, Rav tells his son Chiya, “Seize the opportunity and recite the blessing,” which appears inconsistent with the principle that one who answers Amen is greater than the person reciting the blessing. Ma'adanei Yom Tov answers with difficulty and writes that Rashi, who explains at the end of Kisui HaDam that the forty gold coins correspond to four blessings to which one answers Amen, does not accept Rabbeinu Tam’s rule that the one who answers Amen is greater. His words are not correct. On the contrary, even Rav’s own position proves the essential principle. The Gemara says there that Rav follows the Tanna who holds that both the one reciting the blessing and the one answering Amen are included, except that reward is given more quickly to the person reciting the blessing. Thus even Rav agrees that the one answering Amen receives the same reward; the dispute is only who receives priority. Rabbeinu Tam’s rule that the preemptor is exempt is therefore necessarily true according to everyone, because the person answering Amen still receives the reward of the blessing. How, then, could Rashi disagree? Nor is Ma'adanei Yom Tov’s explanation of Rashi correct. Rather, Rashi’s intent appears to be based upon Rabbi’s language to that person: “Will you drink the cup of blessing, or will you take forty gold coins?” This does not imply that the other person himself would recite Grace After Meals. Had that been the meaning, Rabbi should have said, “Will you recite Grace After Meals?” Tosafot likewise explicitly imply that merely drinking the cup would not itself have earned this reward and that Rabbi intended to dismiss that person. See there. It is also unlikely that Rabbi would have allowed such a person to lead Grace After Meals for his meal. Necessarily, Rabbi meant: “Will you drink the cup of blessing together with us?” The forty gold coins therefore correspond to the blessings to which that person would answer Amen. Accordingly, Rashi actually agrees with Rabbeinu Tam. This appears correct. It is commonly said that one who honors another to lead Grace After Meals is thereby honoring him with forty gold coins. I have heard this in the name of several great authorities. Shiltei HaGibborim in the chapter HaChovel, folio 34a, likewise writes that if a person was invited to lead Grace After Meals and another person preempted him and recited it, the preemptor must pay him forty gold coins. He says this is explicit in the Gemara in Kisui HaDam. Rabbeinu Yerucham in Sefer Meisharim, Netiv 31, end of part 4, likewise writes that one who takes a mitzvah from another must pay ten gold coins, and for a cup of blessing forty. The Gemara in Kisui HaDam, folio 87a, also appears to imply this. Regarding the incident of Rabban Gamliel it asks whether the ten gold coins were compensation for the mitzvah or for the blessing, and asks what practical difference there is for Grace After Meals. The plain implication is that the question concerns one who takes away another person’s opportunity to lead Grace After Meals. It is strained to say that the Gemara merely asks how much reward the person reciting Grace After Meals receives independently of any preemption. Yet a difficulty remains. We have already established that one who answers Amen is greater than the person reciting the blessing, and for this reason Rabbeinu Tam, the Rosh, Mordekhai, and the other authorities exempt one who preempts another mohel, since the latter can answer Amen. In Rabban Gamliel’s case I already explained that the preemptor must have recited the blessing quietly so the other person could not answer Amen. But with Grace After Meals, how can a case arise where a preemptor must pay forty gold coins? If the original person had not been invited to lead, he would still answer Amen to the leader and thereby receive the same forty-gold-coin reward. Rabbeinu Yerucham himself writes that where one can answer Amen, the preemptor is exempt. Even if one says that the preemptor acted improperly and recited Grace After Meals quietly so the other could not answer Amen, the deprived person still has to recite Grace After Meals himself afterward, since the other did not discharge his obligation. He therefore still receives the reward of his own four blessings. It appears that a person earns the ten-gold-coin reward for a blessing only when he recites it before others. A blessing recited privately does not carry that compensable value. Accordingly, the Gemara, Shiltei HaGibborim, and Rabbeinu Yerucham concern a case where the person cannot answer Amen—for example, the preemptor seized the cup of Grace After Meals, pushed him outside, and closed the door until the others had finished. Although the deprived person afterward recites Grace After Meals for himself, he does so privately and therefore has lost the reward associated with leading the public blessing. The same must be true in Rabban Gamliel’s incident: the original slaughterer intended to recite the blessing aloud before others, and the preemptor came first and recited it quietly or in some similar manner. Accordingly, the common saying that simply honoring someone to lead Grace After Meals is equivalent to giving him forty gold coins is not literally correct, because even without leading he can answer Amen. Perhaps the saying means only that one honors him with the priority accorded to the person reciting the blessing, since reward is paid first to the one who blesses, as I wrote above. This still requires study.
Regarding the blessing over Torah reading, see the Rosh and Mordekhai there, who cite Rabbeinu Tam that the preemptor is exempt. Maharshal, chapter HaChovel, siman 60, writes that nowadays, when mitzvah honors are purchased for money, if one purchased the third, sixth, or seventh aliyah and another person preempted him, then if the purchaser seized ten gold coins we do not remove them from him. His words are not compelling. See Maharshal there for several additional distinctions in these matters.

turei_zahav.he: (ס"א) הואיל ועומד לכך דאל"כ לא שבקת חיי לכל אדם שכל א' יזיק חבירו ויאמר ברשותך עשיתי:
turei_zahav.en: He said to him, “I am not in the midst of my life for every man whose father shall be harmed, and I shall say to you.”
